One and done
BARRE — Gary Allen will tell you the main ingredient for a hole-in-one involves a deleted expletive.
“You can’t quote me, but it’s bull-(expletive deleted) luck,” said Allen, who is something of an expert on the subject.
Seems Allen, 76, has been golfing for more than 65 years, and on Tuesday he aced the seventh hole at the Country Club of Barre in Plainfield.
It wasn’t the first time Allen was one and done on the 157-yard par 3, and when it comes to bull-(expletive deleted) luck, the Barre man has had more than his share over the years.
It all started with a hole-in-one Allen notched 25 years or so ago in Rutland. Before hitting the course on Tuesday morning he’d aced three holes — 4, 7 and 16 — at the Country Club of Barre, where he has long been a regular. By the time he took the clubhouse turn, four career holes in one became five and he’d conquered the seventh hole with his hit-it-close-and-hope strategy a second time.
Allen, who sheepishly shared the story, had witnesses. His foursome included Mark Nicholson, Tommy Collins and Gary McQuesten.
Who won? “After you get a hole in one, who cares?” said Allen, who almost left it there.
He didn’t. “I was the loser, because I had to pay the bill when we got back to the bar,” he added. “That’s golf.”
Ready to rock
BARRE — The Vermont Granite Museum has come a long way in the past 30 years. And if you haven’t checked it out recently, you should swing by on Saturday.
Since 1997, the museum on Jones Brothers Way has hosted an annual Granite Festival, like the one that should draw a crowd between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on Saturday.
It’s a season-ending event for the museum, where admission will be free, sculptors Chris Miller and Ryan Mays will both be busy, and you can try your had at everything from modeling clay to sandblasting and etching granite.
Though the festival, like the museum, is largely about the stone, the industry, and the artisans that put Barre on the map, the family-friendly affair will feature fun, games, food, live entertainment and a chance to dunk dignitaries.
“It’s a community celebration,” says Rebecca McLaughlin, who is busy tending to last-minute details, like locking down those dignitaries.
Councilor Michael Deering sounds like he’ll sit for a bit in the dunk tank and, barring an emergency, Police Chief Brad Vail and Fire Chief Keith Cushman are expected to take turns.
Pastor Rae Fraumann from the Hedding United Methodist Church will be playing guitar from 10 to 11 a.m., and the VT Bluegrass Pioneers will be on the main stage from 1 to 3 p.m.
Tasty Bites will be selling food. Rep. Michael Boutin will be wandering about making complimentary balloon animals. And folks can hop in one of the pedal cars, play nine holes of miniature golf, or watch a demonstration by the Stone Trust.
The weather looks like it’s going to cooperate, but this is always a rain-or-shine event. Having a huge roof, like the museum now housed in what’s left of what was once Barre’s largest granite manufacturing plant, has come in handy over the years.
Blue Crew
BERLIN — It should be pretty quiet at Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Vermont’s offices in Berlin today because all of its employees will be donning their “Blue Crew” shirts to pitch in elsewhere.
The focus of today’s all-employee “Day of Service” is food security — an issue that impacts two out of five Vermonters, and has ripple effects in their communities.
So, what will the Blue Crew do, and where will they do it?
That depends. There are hundreds of them, and they’ll be out gleaning fields, cleaning produce, sorting and packing food, and preparing meals for Vermonters who need them.
A handful of volunteers are predictably headed to the Vermont Foodbank in Barre Town’s Wilson Industrial Park. More than 100 will be dispatched to the Intervale Center in Burlington. They will be gleaning, weeding and processing food at those locations, as well as other organizations whose mission is to provide healthy food to those who need it.
Of course, the Blue Crew will shed their work shirts, and return to work on Friday, when it will be back to business as usual at Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Vermont.
Unsolved mystery
BARRE — It wasn’t for lack of trying, but pinpointing what claimed the lives of more than 380 fish on a short stretch of Gunners Brook last week, wasn’t possible.
The fish, which ranged from fingerlings to seven-inch trout, were found, mouths agape, floating in the vicinity of Seminary Street last Thursday.
The thinking is something that shouldn’t have gone into the brook did, but the number of possible sources was so large that finding out just how it happened wasn’t possible.
A floor drain or sump pump in the densely populated neighborhood is viewed as the most likely conduit for whatever chemical caused the fish kill to make its way into the brook.
Ryan McCall, chief environmental enforcement officer for the state Department of Environmental Conservation, was among those who responded.
“We spent an exorbitant amount of time trying to figure it out,” he says, noting there were a thousand possibilities on that stretch of the brook.
“It could have come from anywhere,” he said.
Whether inadvertent, or accidental, McCall says folks should be extra cautious when it comes to storing, handling and, particularly, disposing of cleaning supplies because Vermont’s rivers aren’t wastewater systems.
“Please do not pour cleaning chemicals down floor drains that you don’t know are connected to a municipal wastewater system,” he says.
That appears to be what happened in Barre last week, and nearly 400 fish are dead as a result.
